hops.title: The manatee's smooth but layered brain
hops.text: Florida manatees have one of the largest naturally smooth brains of any animal: about the size of a grapefruit, roughly 360 grams, with a folding score of 1.06 against about 5 in whales and dolphins. Zoologists call it lissencephalic, the same word used for the human disorder. Yet in parts of the manatee's frontal cortex the neurons sit in six well-defined layers, with dense clusters in layer six thought to handle touch from the bristles around its mouth. In classic human lissencephaly the cortex is typically four-layered instead. Both brains can look smooth; their layers tell different stories.

hops.afterHeading: Too few: a tape measure and a spindle
hops.title: A fossil skull and the microcephaly debate
hops.text: LB1, the fossil that defines Homo floresiensis, was an adult, probably female, who stood about a meter tall; Falk's team measured its braincase at 417 cubic centimeters. Critics proposed she was a modern human with microcephaly, not a new species. In 2007 Dean Falk and colleagues compared CT-based casts of the inside of the braincase from nine microcephalic and ten unaffected people; their shape measures sorted the groups perfectly and put LB1 with the unaffected. In 2011 another team revisited those same two shape measures with new comparison groups and found LB1 within the range of casts from people with microcephaly, evidence they called short of proof.

hops.afterHeading: In the wrong place: lissencephaly and the double cortex
hops.title: Why nearly every calico cat is female
hops.text: Meet a calico or tortoiseshell cat and guess female; you will almost always be right. Orange coat color was long known to be X-linked; in May 2025 two teams published peer-reviewed papers online explaining it: a missing stretch of about 5,000 DNA letters that switches on ARHGAP36 in pigment cells and shifts them toward orange. In a female with one orange X and one dark X, each early embryonic cell silences one X at random and passes that choice on, so her coat grows in orange and dark patches; the white comes from a separate gene. The same random choice gives a DCX carrier a mosaic cortex.
